doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

chapter: Life and work in New York
title: Living in New York, getting club work and the union
summary: New York is her base, work goes through representatives, and the union matters little.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Have you both lived in — New York has been your base?
Yeah I’ve been there about 20 years.
Has it ever occurred to you that you’d want to go somewhere else?
I can’t think of where else I could be. It’s where my whole family is from to be honest. And it’s where I feel I have to be musically. I don’t know, I couldn’t think of any other place at the moment.
But you had said that as far as playing right in New York, do you play a lot in New York?
Here and there. It’s not as frequent as you would think. But the work is generated often because I’m there, which is a strange kind of contradiction but that’s just the way it is.
What’s the competition like? Let’s suppose you’ve got a good quartet of people and you’d really like to get them into the Iridium or something. How do you go about that?

Well your reputation has to speak for itself. I mean your recordings and the recognition that you get through them, and your playing and your acceptance among the jazz community and the music business community. Usually that has a lot more to do with it than the acceptance among the music community, the music business community. And then you have to have a solid reputation about what you do and I think time helps, people know and see your body of work over a period of time.
Do you call the club yourself? © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
No, no, no, no. You always work through representatives when it comes to that kind of thing.
Right. They don’t want to talk to the artists.

I mean I was interested one day to pick up the book from the New York — I guess it’s 802, the Local, and look at the number of saxophone players in there. It’s like how do all these people work? I suppose some of them are part timers.
There’s a lot of musicians that aren’t even in that book. Yeah there’s a lot of great musicians in New York City. That’s what makes it the interesting place that it is too, so yeah.
Does the musician’s union have a part in what you do at all?
No. No I don’t have much to do with it at all.
It used to be I guess really quite powerful.
Yeah. Not so anymore. Not particularly in the underground jazz world.
